test_text.title: HOW DOES THE BIOLOGICAL CLOCK TICK?

article.title: HOW DOES THE BIOLOGICAL CLOCK TICK?

items.sentence_raw: Our life span is restricted.
Everyone accepts this as 'biologically' obvious.
"Nothing lives for ever!"
However, in this statement we think of artificially produced, technical objects, products which are subjected to natural wear and tear during use.
This leads to the result that at some time or other the object stops working and is unusable ('death' in the biological sense).
But are the wear and tear and loss of function of technical objects and the death of living organisms really similar or comparable?
items.explain:
Q27: The passage asks if the *'wear and tear'* of objects and the *'death'* of organisms are *'really similar or comparable?'* — this shows the paragraph is about **differences** in ageing. The heading **ix** (*'Fundamental differences in ageing of objects and organisms'*) matches this core question exactly. So the answer is **ix**.

Q37: The passage questions if wear and tear theory is *'really similar or comparable'* for both, and later says the law is *'not inexorable in the same way'* for living things — **'not inexorable'** means it does not work the same. This shows the theory does **not** apply equally, so the statement is false. The answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Our 'dead' products are 'static', closed systems.
It is always the basic material which constitutes the object and which, in the natural course of things, is worn down and becomes 'older'.
Ageing in this case must occur according to the laws of physical chemistry and of thermodynamics.
items.explain:
Q33: The passage says ageing of objects follows *'the laws of physical chemistry and of thermodynamics'* — the first principle is **'physical chemistry'**. So the answer is **physical chemistry**.

Q34: The same sentence gives the second principle: *'thermodynamics'*. So the answer is **thermodynamics**.

items.sentence_raw: Although the same law holds for a living organism, the result of this law is not inexorable in the same way.
items.explain: Q37: The passage questions if wear and tear theory is *'really similar or comparable'* for both, and later says the law is *'not inexorable in the same way'* for living things — **'not inexorable'** means it does not work the same. This shows the theory does **not** apply equally, so the statement is false. The answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: At least as long as a biological system has the ability to renew itself it could actually become older without ageing; an organism is an open, dynamic system through which new material continuously flows.
items.explain: Q38: The passage says a biological system *'could actually become older without ageing'* if it can renew itself — this directly confirms the statement. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Destruction of old material and formation of new material are thus in permanent dynamic equilibrium.
The material of which the organism is formed changes continuously.
Thus our bodies continuously exchange old substance for new, just like a spring which more or less maintains its form and movement, but in which the water molecules are always different.
Thus ageing and death should not be seen as inevitable, particularly as the organism possesses many mechanisms for repair.
It is not, in principle, necessary for a biological system to age and die.
Nevertheless, a restricted life span, ageing, and then death are basic characteristics of life.
The reason for this is easy to recognise: in nature, the existent organisms either adapt or are regularly replaced by new types.

Because of changes in the genetic material (mutations) these have new characteristics and in the course of their individual lives they are tested for optimal or better adaptation to the environmental conditions.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says organisms with mutations are tested for *'optimal or better adaptation to the environmental conditions'* — **'adaptation'** is the noun form, and the question needs the verb **'adapt'**. So the answer is **adapt**.

items.sentence_raw: Immortality would disturb this system - it needs room for new and better life.
items.explain:
Q28: The passage says *'Immortality would disturb this system - it needs room for new and better life'* — **'immortality'** means living forever, and the passage explains why it is bad for evolution. The heading **ii** (*'Why dying is beneficial'*) captures this idea — **'beneficial'** means helpful or good. So the answer is **ii**.

Q36: The passage states *'Immortality would disturb this system'* — **'immortality'** is the thing that causes the problem for evolution. So the answer is **immortality**.

items.sentence_raw: This is the basic problem of evolution.
Every organism has a life span which is highly characteristic.
There are striking differences in life span between different species, but within one species the parameter is relatively constant.
For example, the average duration of human life has hardly changed in thousands of years.
items.explain: Q29: The passage states that human life span *'has hardly changed in thousands of years'* and the *'upper limit for most remains 80 years'* despite better medicine and food. This means the life span is **stable** even with **improvements** — exactly what heading **vii** (*'A stable life span despite improvements'*) says. So the answer is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: Although more and more people attain an advanced age as a result of developments in medical care and better nutrition, the characteristic upper limit for most remains 80 years.
items.explain: Q29: The passage states that human life span *'has hardly changed in thousands of years'* and the *'upper limit for most remains 80 years'* despite better medicine and food. This means the life span is **stable** even with **improvements** — exactly what heading **vii** (*'A stable life span despite improvements'*) says. So the answer is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: A further argument against the simple wear and tear theory is the observation that the time within which organisms age lies between a few days (even a few hours for unicellular organisms) and several thousand years, as with mammoth trees.

If a life span is a genetically determined biological characteristic, it is logically necessary to propose the existence of an internal clock, which in some way measures and controls the ageing process and which finally determines death as the last step in a fixed programme.
items.explain: Q30: The passage proposes *'the existence of an internal clock, which in some way measures and controls the ageing process'* — this **'internal clock'** is the same idea as a **'biological clock'**. Heading **i** (*'The biological clock'*) directly names this concept. So the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: Like the life span, the metabolic rate has for different organisms a fixed mathematical relationship to the body mass.
In comparison to the life span this relationship is 'inverted': the larger the organism the lower its metabolic rate.
Again this relationship is valid not only for birds, but also, similarly on average within the systematic unit, for all other organisms (plants, animals, unicellular organisms).
Animals which behave 'frugally' with energy become particularly old, for example, crocodiles and tortoises.
items.explain: Q31: The paragraph gives many examples: animals that are *'frugally'* with energy live longer, and higher *'metabolic rate'* in men leads to shorter life. All these examples focus on how **energy use** affects life span — which matches heading **viii** (*'Energy consumption'*). So the answer is **viii**.

items.sentence_raw: Parrots and birds of prey are often held chained up.
Thus they are not able to 'experience life' and so they attain a high life span in captivity.
Animals which save energy by hibernation or lethargy (e.g. bats or hedgehogs) live much longer than those which are always active.
items.explain: Q31: The paragraph gives many examples: animals that are *'frugally'* with energy live longer, and higher *'metabolic rate'* in men leads to shorter life. All these examples focus on how **energy use** affects life span — which matches heading **viii** (*'Energy consumption'*). So the answer is **viii**.

items.sentence_raw: The metabolic rate of mice can be reduced by a very low consumption of food (hunger diet).
They then may live twice as long as their well fed comrades.
Women become distinctly (about 10 per cent) older than men.
If you examine the metabolic rates of the two sexes you establish that the higher male metabolic rate roughly accounts for the lower male life span.
items.explain: Q31: The paragraph gives many examples: animals that are *'frugally'* with energy live longer, and higher *'metabolic rate'* in men leads to shorter life. All these examples focus on how **energy use** affects life span — which matches heading **viii** (*'Energy consumption'*). So the answer is **viii**.

items.sentence_raw: That means that they live life 'energetically' - more intensively, but not for as long.
It follows from the above that sparing use of energy reserves should tend to extend life.
items.explain:
Q32: The passage says *'sparing use of energy reserves should tend to extend life'* and suggests making your own *'energy saving programme'* — this is advice on how to make life longer. Heading **iv** (*'Prolonging your life'*) means exactly that — **'prolonging'** means making longer. So the answer is **iv**.

Q40: The passage concludes that *'sparing use of energy reserves should tend to extend life'* — **'sparing use'** means **'conserving'**, and **'extend life'** means **'help to extend a human's life'**. This matches the statement exactly. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Extreme high performance sports may lead to optimal cardiovascular performance, but they quite certainly do not prolong life.
Relaxation lowers metabolic rate, as does adequate sleep and in general an equable and balanced personality.
Each of us can develop his or her own 'energy saving programme' with a little self-observation, critical self-control and, above all, logical consistency.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says *'sparing use of energy reserves should tend to extend life'* and suggests making your own *'energy saving programme'* — this is advice on how to make life longer. Heading **iv** (*'Prolonging your life'*) means exactly that — **'prolonging'** means making longer. So the answer is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: Experience will show that to live in this way not only increases the life span but is also very healthy.
This final aspect should not be forgotten.

orphan_explain_map.39: Q39: The passage talks about bodies exchanging old substance for new, like a spring, but it never gives a specific number like **'90 per cent'** or a time like **'seven years'**. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — the information is simply missing. So the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
